claims.text: The proposed framework will compute electronic and lattice thermal transport separately for HfNbTaTiZr.
The framework will reduce prediction error by approximately 30% relative to previous Debye-based aggregated models.
The material states considered are ideal defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Electronic transport will be modeled using many-body perturbation theory, possible GW corrections, and Boltzmann transport calculations.
Lattice transport will be modeled using anharmonic phonon solvers and ab initio molecular dynamics in large supercells.
Explicit oxygen defects affect both phonon scattering and the local electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable below 200 K.
The modeled alloy is assumed to remain a single-phase BCC structure without phase transitions over the stated temperature range.
Oxygen impurities induce local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Realistic supercell treatment of oxygen-induced local distortions mediates the separation of phonon and electron transport in the simulation.
Separating the electronic and lattice channels avoids reliance on an aggregated Debye-temperature parameter.
Explicit defective-supercell calculations account for defect-induced scattering and temperature-dependent effects neglected by earlier aggregated approaches.
The model will reproduce comparable lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions below 200 K.
For HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, the model will predict total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Previous approaches conflate lattice and electronic contributions, rely on DFT-derived elastic properties or Debye formulas, and assume perfect defect-free crystals.

The expected applicability is limited to single-phase equimolar HfNbTaTiZr and low-level oxygen-doped variants without significant phase transitions or oxygen concentrations above approximately 1 wt.%.
Defect distribution and anharmonic effects may change the exact error reduction achieved by the framework.
Experimental separation of lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions is challenging.
The hypothesis is falsified if predicted total or channel-resolved conductivities differ from measurements by more than 30%, or if the model misses the specified low- and high-temperature behavior.
